title: Human Response to Window Views and Indoor Plants in the Workplace
research_question: To explore the effects of window views (natural vs. urban visual content) and the presence of indoor plants on participants' physiological and state-anxiety well-being in workplace environments.

participants.description: 38 volunteer students (10 males, 28 females) from the Horticulture department at National Chung-Hsing University, Taichung, Taiwan. All participants were in good health.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Six simulated office environments created using Photo Impact 5.0, varying in window view content (city, nature, or none) and presence of indoor plants. Conditions were: 1) no window, no plants (O); 2) no window, with plants (OP); 3) city view, no plants (C); 4) city view, with plants (CP); 5) nature view, no plants (N); 6) nature view, with plants (NP). Indoor plants included Cigar flower, Aglaonema, Common poinsettia. Outdoor plant in nature views was Peepul Tree.

findings.antecedent: Office without window view and no indoor plants
findings.mechanism: Lack of natural elements leads to higher tension and anxiety.
findings.quote: When neither the window view nor the indoor plants were shown, participants suffered the highest degree of tension and anxiety.

findings.antecedent: View of nature and/or indoor plants
findings.mechanism: Exposure to natural elements reduces nervousness and anxiety.
findings.quote: Participants were less nervous or anxious when watching a view of nature and/or when indoor plants were present.

findings.antecedent: Window view of nature
findings.mechanism: Nature views are more effective for stress recovery and cognitive restoration than indoor plants or cityscape views.
findings.quote: a window view of nature is more effective in an office workplace than indoor plants, and that a window with a view of nature has more effect than one of a cityscape.

mechanisms: Stress recovery: Nature and plants facilitate recovery from mental fatigue and stress.
Cognitive restoration: Soft beauty in nature enhances mental health and provides opportunities for cognitive restoration.

Physiological regulation: Emotional and cognitive responses initiated by the cerebral cortex and limbic system stimulate the hypothalamus-pituitary gland, leading to autonomic nervous system reactions (e.g., changes in brain waves, muscle tension, blood volume pulse).
Relaxed wakefulness: Higher alpha EEG activity is associated with relaxed but wakeful conditions.
implementation_implications: Windows in workplaces provide stress relief and higher satisfaction.
Views of nature (flowers, trees) lead to greater satisfaction and less stress than views of buildings or no views.
Even a small portion of nature in a view can be beneficial.
Artificial nature can also help with stress and anxiety relief.
Combinations of window views and indoor plants can provide more positive well-being in offices.
Providing elements of nature (plants, window views) can help alleviate stress, boredom, and fatigue in office workplaces.
Nature views are generally more effective than indoor plants alone, and nature views are more effective than cityscape views.
Consider plant selection and placement to be consistent with the view outward from windows.
For offices with limited views, planning for larger or higher trees in window views is recommended.
Designing for natural views (30 to 80 ft from rooms) can improve human well-being more than architectural elements alone.

tables.description: Mean and standard deviation of respondents' response values when looking at different pictures of workplace environments (6 conditions: O, OP, C, CP, N, NP) for EEG-a, EEG-b, EMG, BVP, and State-Anxiety, including F-statistics and pairwise comparisons.

Mean and standard deviation of respondents' response values when looking at different workplace environments views, grouped into three categories (O+OP, C+CP, N+NP) for EEG-a, EEG-b, EMG, BVP, and State-Anxiety, including F-statistics and pairwise comparisons.

limitations: The study used a convenience sample of volunteer students from a Horticulture department, which may limit the generalizability of the findings to a broader population.
The study used simulated office environments (photographs) rather than real physical spaces, which may not fully capture the complexity and dynamic nature of actual workplaces.
